proof_summary: An identity for the factorial sums, followed by parity and coprimality cancellations, rewrites the term as \(Q=B/\gcd(B,(n-3)!)\), where \(B=(n^2-2)/\gcd(n^2-2,2)\). Every prime divisor \(p\mid B\) is at least \(7\); if \(Q\) were composite, its least prime divisor would give \(p^2\le Q\), while factorial valuations and \(((k+1)p+2)^2<p^{k+2}\) for \(k=\lfloor(n-3)/p\rfloor\) contradict \(B<n^2\), with the remaining near-\(n\) prime cases excluded directly by divisibility.
